I keep thinking I should’ve done more, that maybe if I’d gone back in a second time, things would’ve been different. I know it’s not rational, but I can’t shake this guilt, like I deserve to be punished somehow. 

Most days, I feel… hollow. It’s like I’m watching life from behind glass. My wife says I’ve been distant, and I hate that I can’t pull myself together for her. I want to care, but the emotions just don’t come. Even when I sit down, I can’t stay still—my legs bounce, I pace the living room at night, pick at my hands until they’re raw. 

I catch myself wishing I wouldn’t wake up some mornings. Not because I want to end it, but because it just feels easier than facing another day like this. I still go to shifts, but I’m not present. I make mistakes I never used to. It’s more than just reacting to what happened—it’s like this weight won’t let go, no matter what I do.
D013-D020_h004.question_b:
I’ve been feeling off ever since my best friend and fellow firefighter died in a collapse during a rescue call—about five months ago now. It happened three months into me being back on full duty after recovering from my own injuries. Since then, I can’t seem to shake this heaviness. I don’t cry, but I don’t really feel much of anything—just numb. My wife says I’m distant, like I’m not all there.

I can’t sit still, even when I’m off the rig. I pace around the house at night, wring my hands, sometimes pick at my arms until they’re raw. I keep thinking it should’ve been me—like I should’ve pulled him out or gone in differently. I catch myself thinking, *“I wish I wouldn’t wake up,”* not because I want to end things, but because it feels easier than carrying this guilt.

It’s affected my work, too—I’m slow, distracted. But honestly, it’s not like I’ve lost interest in everything. I still care about my crew, my wife, the job. I just can’t seem to process it. Everything changed after that call—this all started within weeks.
